title: Capturing, Non-Capturing Groups & Backreferences
description: Master memory management in regex. Extract targeted data with capturing groups, optimize performance with non-capturing groups, and match recurring structural patterns with backreferences.

primer.definition: Parentheses create capturing groups (...) that store matched substrings in memory. Adding ?: creates a non-capturing group (?:...) for grouping without memory overhead. Backreferences (\1, \2) allow you to re-match whatever was captured in a previous group.
primer.goldenRule: Use non-capturing groups (?:...) when you only need logical grouping (like alternation or quantifiers) without capturing data into memory. Use backreferences (\1) when a future part of your pattern must match the exact same value captured earlier.
primer.mentalModel: Think of a capturing group as a labeled sticky note the regex engine writes as it reads through your string. A backreference like \1 tells the engine to peek back at that sticky note and demand the exact same text appear again -- it's a memory lookup, not a re-run of the original pattern.
points: Groups are numbered left-to-right by their opening parenthesis, starting at 1; group 0 always refers to the entire match.
(?:...) groups for logic (alternation, quantifiers) without allocating a capture slot -- use it whenever you don't need to reference the matched text later.
A backreference \1 re-matches the literal text captured by group 1, not the pattern that captured it -- (\d{3})\1 means 'the exact same three digits again', not 'any three more digits'.
Named groups (?<name>...) and named backreferences \k<name> behave identically to numbered groups but make patterns self-documenting once a pattern has more than two or three groups.
pitfalls: Confusing \1 with repeating the pattern: (\d{3})\1 matches "123123", not any three digits followed by any three digits -- \1 requires the exact same characters that were captured, not the same shape.
Backreferences are case-sensitive by default: (\w)\1 matches "aa" but not "aA" -- add the i flag if you want case-insensitive backreference matching.

A group inside an unmatched alternation branch or an optional quantifier (e.g. (?:(a)|b)) may never capture at all, leaving its backreference undefined rather than an empty string -- test every branch.
Named backreference syntax is easy to typo: \k<name> (with the k) is required -- referencing it as \<name> or \name silently fails to work as intended in most engines.

cards.prompt: Create a capturing group for the word 'cat'.
Group 'cat' or 'dog' without capturing using (?:cat|dog).
Match a digit captured in group 1, followed by a space and the same digit using backreference \1.
Match 'http' or 'https' using a non-capturing group, followed by '://'.
Match 'abc' repeated one or more times strictly from start to end using a non-capturing group.
Match HTML-style tags like text ensuring opening and closing tag names match using \1.
Match a string wrapped in either matching single or double quotes strictly from start to end using backreference \1.
